stories.title: APAC data centers pivot to AI, high-density capacity: JLL
stories.summary: Mikhael Jaura, JLL's Head of Data Center Research for Asia Pacific, stated that mature APAC data center hubs are reorienting around AI-ready, high-density capacity. New markets like Mumbai and Chennai are developing at hyperscale. The region's diverse landscape presents both opportunities and challenges for investors.
stories.why_it_matters: A major broker's read on the market confirms that AI density requirements, not generic colocation demand, now drive site selection and design across APAC. Investors face a split market: paying premiums for retrofittable capacity in established hubs, or accepting execution and regulatory risk in fast-scaling newer markets like India.
stories.content:
Mikhael Jaura, JLL's Head of Data Center Research for Asia Pacific, noted that the APAC data center market is no longer a single story.Mature hubs are reinventing themselves to support AI-ready, high-density capacity. Markets such as Mumbai, Chennai, Johor, Batam, and Seoul’s periphery are being developed at hyperscale.
### Market Dynamics and Constraints

Demand fundamentals in Japan remain resilient, driven by cloud and AI adoption. Supply is not keeping pace, however.Grid connection timelines in Greater Tokyo and Osaka are reaching ten years. Construction cost inflation and a squeezed labour market are lengthening delivery schedules, pushing development to secondary regions like Hokkaido and Kyushu.In Hong Kong, sentiment has improved due to demand from Mainland Chinese hyperscalers. The market positions itself as a connectivity gateway to the Greater Bay Area through the Northern Metropolis.Powered land is a binding constraint in Hong Kong. Absorption slowed in 2025 but rebounded, driven by AI demand from Mainland Chinese technology firms.China is building a self-contained AI stack, encompassing domestic accelerators and national compute programmes such as “East Data, West Computing.” This programme designates eight national computing hubs and ten data center clusters, moving new capacity to western provinces where land, renewable power, and cooling are cheaper.South Korea is transitioning from a Seoul-centric market to national AI infrastructure. Policy is pushing new capacity south due to grid capacity constraints in the capital region.The AIDC Special Act, effective in Q1 2027, will fast-track permitting outside Seoul. Regional electricity pricing proposed in August 2026 would offer discounts of up to 10 per cent in the south.Malaysia's Johor capacity has grown more than 50-fold since 2020, with 1,800 MW under construction. Greater Kuala Lumpur is becoming a cloud market, with Microsoft, AWS, and Google establishing regions there.Indonesia has a large digital economy, data localisation rules, and hyperscaler cloud regions in Greater Jakarta. Batam offers a cross-border option for demand from Singapore.
### Enterprise Demand and Key Markets

Enterprise demand is maturing towards hybrid and multi-cloud architectures. Regulated, latency-sensitive, and AI inference workloads are staying in colocation near cloud on-ramps.Data residency is a major driver in India, where vacancy fell to a record 2.8 per cent in H1 2026. Mumbai’s growth is driven mainly by domestic demand due to residency rules bringing workloads onshore.Mumbai is expected to take 35 per cent of India’s 4.4 GW pipeline by 2029. Chennai offers competitive colocation power costs at around 8.4 US cents per kWh compared to 18.1 cents in Singapore.
### Operational Challenges

AI accelerator refresh cycles have compressed sharply, to as little as 13 months. Older chips are still used for inference and fine-tuning, where cost per token matters more than peak speed.Facilities typically need major power or cooling upgrades within 18 to 36 months to host the next generation of chips. Designing flexible facilities is a priority to support several chip generations over their lifetime.Captive and dedicated power generation units are expected to become more common. Hybrid models will combine grid power with dedicated renewables, on-site generation, and storage.Water access has become a permitting criterion. Johor has enforced tighter controls, and Australia restricts potable water for cooling, requiring recycled or alternative sources. Thailand is reviewing water usage in its national standards for data centers.Hyperscale occupiers are asking detailed questions about cooling design, water usage effectiveness (WUE), and water sourcing during the Request for Proposal (RFP) stage. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling for AI generally helps on both power and water consumption, particularly in closed-loop systems.

# APAC data centers pivot to AI, high-density capacity: JLL

Mikhael Jaura, JLL's Head of Data Center Research for Asia Pacific, stated that mature APAC data center hubs are reorienting around AI-ready, high-density capacity. New markets like Mumbai and Chennai are developing at hyperscale. The region's diverse landscape presents both opportunities and challenges for investors.

- Published On Oct 17, 2026 at 07:56 AM IST

## Highlights

- Mature APAC hubs are reorienting for AI-ready, high-density data center capacity.
- Mumbai and Chennai are developing as hyperscale markets within India's growing sector.
- Japan and Hong Kong face constraints like grid connection delays and limited powered land.
- Water access and accelerated chip refresh cycles are driving new design and power strategies.

stories.title: Delta unveils AI modular data centre for NVIDIA Vera Rubin
stories.summary: Operators in Southeast Asia could speed AI capacity builds as Delta's modular system pairs liquid cooling with 800 VDC power for NVIDIA Vera Rubin.
stories.why_it_matters: Modular, factory-integrated systems aligned to NVIDIA's roadmap shorten deployment cycles for AI builds, which matters most in Southeast Asian markets where grid connections and construction timelines are the binding constraints. Equipment vendors that certify early against Vera Rubin-class power and cooling requirements gain an advantage in the region's AI infrastructure race.
stories.content:
Fri, 16th Oct 2026 (Yesterday)
Delta Electronics has unveiled an AI modular data centre with an 800 VDC in-row power system built for NVIDIA Vera Rubin. It also presented a microgrid system for powering AI data centres in Southeast Asia.

The modular system combines prefabricated data centre infrastructure with liquid cooling and a direct current power architecture for high-density AI computing deployments.

Delta said the AI Modular Data Centre integrates an 800 VDC in-row power design with liquid cooling to support installations based on NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture. The system is intended to speed deployment and expansion as operators in the region face rising demand for computing capacity.

Delta disclosed several technical details of the power setup. The 800 VDC in-row architecture delivers 660kW of output power, up to 98% AC-DC efficiency and 480kW of battery backup capacity. It also uses aluminium capacitors in a design intended to support GPU workloads in next-generation AI data centres.

Alongside the modular data centre, Delta outlined its approach to energy supply for AI facilities through a separate microgrid offering. The system combines renewable energy, energy storage, solid oxide fuel cell systems and solid state transformers.

According to the company, the solid state transformer is designed to convert medium-voltage electricity directly to 800 VDC. The microgrid system can coordinate multiple energy sources in real time to maintain uptime and power quality during grid connection delays or off-grid operation, while the fuel cell system provides around-the-clock on-site power.

The microgrid design uses a prefabricated DC-coupled architecture that combines solid state transformers, DC/DC converters and dynamic energy support. Delta said this reduces conversion stages and allows the system to respond to fluctuating AI loads while supporting larger deployments.

### Regional demand

The launch comes as Singapore and the wider Southeast Asia market attract growing investment in AI infrastructure. Data centre operators across the region are under pressure to add capacity quickly and accommodate much higher rack densities than in previous deployment cycles.

Delta is positioning its offering around that shift, combining electrical infrastructure, cooling systems and on-site power resources in a single package. The company also highlighted a prefabricated AI containerised data centre product that can deliver up to 60kW per rack of AI compute within the footprint of a single parking space.

The containerised design also includes an integrated liquid-to-air coolant distribution unit system. Delta said it can achieve a power usage effectiveness rating as low as 1.19.

At board level, the company also disclosed a thermal management product designed for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72. It said the cold plate uses a microchannel and multi-impinging flow design.

The broader push reflects a change in how suppliers to the data centre sector are framing AI infrastructure projects. Rather than focusing only on servers and racks, vendors are increasingly presenting complete systems that combine power conversion, battery backup, thermal management and on-site generation.

That trend is particularly visible in AI deployments, where high-density clusters create heavier and less predictable electricity and cooling loads. In Southeast Asia, those pressures are colliding with grid constraints, land limits and rising scrutiny over the energy use of digital infrastructure.

Jason Yuan, President, Southeast Asia & ANZ, Delta Electronics, said the demands created by AI are forcing a rethink in infrastructure planning.

"AI workloads are scaling faster than most data centres were designed to handle, while their demands can be increasingly unpredictable. This means infrastructure planning must move from reactive to integrated and future-ready," said Jason Yuan, President, Southeast Asia & ANZ, Delta Electronics.

He added: "Our AI Modular Data Centres and Microgrids, both part of our Grid-to-Chip Solutions portfolio, are ideal to help our clients across Southeast Asia deploy and power their future-ready AI data centers. Moreover, Delta's solutions are engineered for energy efficiency, reliability and performance, while providing the flexibility to adapt to changing workloads and infrastructure demands."
stories.title_zh: Delta发布面向NVIDIA Vera Rubin的AI模块化数据中心
stories.summary_zh: 随着Delta的模块化系统将液冷与800 VDC供电相结合以支持NVIDIA Vera Rubin，东南亚的运营商有望加快AI容量建设。
stories.why_zh: 与NVIDIA路线图对齐的模块化、工厂集成系统可缩短AI建设的部署周期，这在电网接入和施工周期构成瓶颈约束的东南亚市场尤为重要。率先针对Vera Rubin级功率和冷却要求完成认证的设备供应商，将在该地区的AI基础设施竞赛中占据优势。

stories.title: CHINT unveils factory-built Power Pod for Asia data centres
stories.summary: Data centre developers in Asia-Pacific could cut installation times by up to 60% as CHINT's factory-built power pod targets AI-driven demand.
stories.why_it_matters: Prefabricated power systems shift work off constrained construction sites and into factories, directly attacking the schedule risk that delays APAC data center deliveries. A lower-cost Chinese supplier entering this segment also pressures incumbents on price, giving developers more procurement options as AI builds strain electrical supply chains.
stories.content:
Fri, 16th Oct 2026 (Yesterday)
CHINT has introduced its factory-built Power Pod for the Asian market and given an early preview of its Solid-State Transformer technology.

The launch comes as data centre operators in Asia-Pacific face growing pressure to secure electrical equipment for AI-led expansion.

The Power Pod is a containerised system that combines switchgear, transformer and circuit protection in one enclosed unit for outdoor installation. It also includes cooling, fire protection, lighting and security, and is assembled and tested before shipment.

CHINT said the product can cut on-site installation time by up to 60% compared with field-built systems, with deployment taking as little as one week after the unit reaches a site.

Configurations range from 500kW to 4,000kW, which CHINT said is enough to support anything from a single high-density AI rack to roughly a full data hall.

The company is positioning the product as a response to a problem that has become more acute as AI workloads increase electricity demand in data centres. Operators are not only expanding computing capacity, but also trying to secure and integrate power infrastructure quickly enough to keep projects on schedule.

CHINT said most of the Power Pod's core equipment is manufactured and tested in-house rather than sourced from several vendors and assembled on site. The equipment is validated at its 4MW in-house testing facility before shipment.

The approach is intended to reduce supplier handoffs and leave one manufacturer responsible for production, integration and testing. CHINT said this can shorten the gap between equipment delivery and energising a data hall.

Lead times for key components remain a challenge across the sector. Large power transformers, among the longest-lead items in a new data centre build, are taking roughly 128 weeks to deliver, according to CHINT.

According to figures cited by the company from Cushman & Wakefield's Data Centre Advisory Group, Asia-Pacific data centre capacity is projected to increase 2.4 times, with 13.8GW of operational capacity and a further 19.4GW under construction or planned.

Paul Lee, APAC Strategic Segment Director at CHINT, said the issue is no longer simply adding more servers.

"Power is now the hardest part of building AI infrastructure," said Paul Lee, APAC Strategic Segment Director at CHINT.

"Operators don't need another pile of components to integrate, wire and commission on site - they need a single, factory-validated power block they can install and switch on. That's the problem our Power Pod is built to solve," Lee said.

### DC architecture

Alongside the Power Pod, CHINT outlined its Solid-State Transformer, or SST, as part of a direct current architecture for data centres. The system uses power electronics and high-frequency components to convert medium-voltage alternating current from the grid directly into 800V direct current for AI data centre environments, according to the company.

CHINT said the SST has a stated peak efficiency of up to 98.5% and a power factor of at least 0.99. It added that power can move in both directions through the system.

The company described the product as a building block for future high-voltage direct current data centre designs. The aim is to reduce the number of conversion stages between the grid and the IT rack, cutting associated energy losses.

The announcement reflects a broader shift in data centre design as operators seek to manage denser computing loads and the electricity systems that support them. Power distribution equipment, grid connection and final distribution at the rack are drawing more scrutiny as developers try to avoid delays in bringing facilities online.

CHINT said its approach spans grid connection, medium-voltage distribution and final distribution at the IT load, rather than treating each stage as a separate product purchase. It combines electrical systems, engineering, manufacturing and testing within one delivery model.

That model is aimed at data centre developers seeking fewer supplier interfaces and less on-site assembly. In a market where power infrastructure schedules can determine when new computing capacity becomes available, the ability to pre-build and test systems off site is becoming more significant.
stories.title_zh: 正泰（CHINT）推出面向亚洲数据中心的预制化Power Pod电力模块
stories.summary_zh: 随着CHINT面向AI驱动需求推出工厂预制的电力模块（power pod），亚太地区的数据中心开发商有望将安装时间最多缩短60%。
stories.why_zh: 预制电力系统将工作从受限的施工现场转移到工厂，直接化解了拖累亚太数据中心交付的工期风险。一家成本更低的中国供应商进入这一细分市场，也将在价格上对现有厂商形成压力，让开发商在AI建设令电力供应链承压之际拥有更多采购选择。

stories.title: Vietnam's CMC and Korea's Lotte partner to develop data centers
stories.summary: Companies sign MoU to collaborate on data center projects
stories.why_it_matters: The tie-up adds a credible new contender to Vietnam's emerging data center market, where demand is rising on data localization rules and cloud adoption but local players often lack the capital to build at scale. For Korean conglomerates, it is another channel into Southeast Asian digital infrastructure as their home market matures.
stories.content:
Vietnam’s CMC is set to partner with South Korea’s Lotte to develop data centers.

CMC and Lotte Innovate this week officially entered into a strategic partnership, signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) around infrastructure, software development, and other areas of mutual interest.

Areas of cooperation under the MoU include data centers, EV charging, security, offshoring, and cloud.

In the data center segment, the companies said they aim to develop data center projects, combining CMC’s infrastructure and operations strengths in Vietnam with Lotte Innovate’s experience and customer ecosystem.

Details of any planned data centers haven’t been shared.

Minh Tran Van, CEO of CMC Korea, said: “Our partnership with Lotte Innovate goes beyond a step in CMC’s global expansion strategy. It reflects the growing role of CMC Korea in connecting Vietnam’s technology capabilities with Korea’s leading corporations. We expect the two sides to not only deliver high-quality software development services together, but also co-create scalable digital solutions across Vietnam, Korea, and regional markets, as demand for digital transformation and AI adoption continues to accelerate across the region.”

Founded in 1993, CMC Corp is one of Vietnam’s largest technology companies. It operates CMC Telecom, one of the major telecoms firms in the country, and offers cloud services through CMC Cloud. The company has data centers in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City.

Lotte Innovate is part of the South Korean Lotte Corporation conglomerate. Founded in 1967, Lotte’s businesses span food, hotels, retail, financial services, chemicals, IT, construction, publishing, and more.

Choi Jong Pil, general director of Lotte Innovate Vietnam, said: “Vietnam is a key market in Lotte Innovate’s global strategy. Through this partnership agreement with CMC Corporation, we aim to combine the strengths of both sides and explore new opportunities in advanced technology areas, contributing to digital transformation and AI adoption for businesses in Vietnam and the region.”

Founded in 1996 and formerly known as Lotte Data Communication, Lotte Innovate provides IT and cloud services. The firm operates four data centers in South Korea around Seoul, Daejeon, and Yongin, offering cloud services via L.Cloud.

The company is also set to take over the operation of Ansan GCC, a 40MW data center building built by Igis Asset Management in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province, that is due live next year.
stories.title_zh: 越南CMC与韩国乐天（Lotte）合作开发数据中心
stories.summary_zh: 两家公司签署谅解备忘录，将在数据中心项目上开展合作
stories.why_zh: 此次合作为越南新兴的数据中心市场增添了一个可信的新竞争者。在数据本地化法规和云服务普及的推动下，当地需求正在上升，但本土企业往往缺乏大规模建设的资金。对韩国企业集团而言，这是在本土市场趋于成熟之际，进入东南亚数字基础设施的又一条渠道。

stories.title: Schneider Electric raises 2026 targets on AI data centre demand
stories.summary: Schneider Electric has increased its 2026 revenue and profit targets for the second time this year, citing strong demand from AI data centres. The company now forecasts higher organic growth for both adjusted earnings and revenue.
stories.content:
Schneider Electric has raised its 2026 core profit and revenue targets for the second time this year, the company announced on Friday.The French industrial group now expects its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation to grow between 18 per cent and 21 per cent organically in 2026. This is an increase from its earlier forecast of 14 per cent to 19 per cent.Organic revenue growth estimations have also been revised to range from 12 per cent to 14 per cent, up from the previous range of 10 per cent to 13 per cent. This growth is primarily fuelled by a surge in demand from major cloud corporations building AI data centres.Schneider Electric, known for its industrial electrical equipment, has become a significant beneficiary of the AI boom. It supplies critical infrastructure for data centres, including cooling units, server racks, and power distribution equipment.CEO Olivier Blum stated that "Data Centres remained a key growth driver as we continue to execute on our backlog while seeing triple-digit demand growth in the quarter." The company's revenue reached a record high of 11.46 billion euros ($12.87 billion) in the third quarter, surpassing analysts' average forecasts.Demand remained healthy across all four end-markets, supporting another record backlog, Blum added. Orders for data centre power, cooling, and automation equipment are sustained by strong demand from US hyperscalers. However, third-quarter growth was led by China and East Asia.The data centre business drove growth in these regions, stemming from direct sales to large customers in social media, technology, and digital infrastructure. It also came from domestic and regional co-location customers.

- Energy, Cooling & Sustainability
- 1 min Read

# Schneider Electric raises 2026 targets on AI data centre demand

Schneider Electric has increased its 2026 revenue and profit targets for the second time this year, citing strong demand from AI data centres. The company now forecasts higher organic growth for both adjusted earnings and revenue.

- Adjusted earnings are forecast to grow 18-21 per cent organically, revenue 12-14 per cent.

stories.title: Digital Realty completes structural milestone at South Korean data center
stories.summary: Digital Realty has marked the topping-out of ICN11, its latest data center development in South Korea, with the facility scheduled to become operational in the second half of 2027. ICN11 is intended to address growing demand for data center capacity in South Korea, driven by increased adoption of cloud services, connectivity and artificial intelligence infrastructure. […]
stories.why_it_matters: Locking in 2027 supply in Seoul matters because land and power constraints make new capacity in the metro scarce, and pre-leasing typically begins well before delivery. The milestone signals Digital Realty is committed to Korea as a core APAC growth market even as competitors crowd into Tokyo, Osaka, and Johor.
stories.content:
Digital Realty has marked the topping-out of ICN11, its latest data center development in South Korea, with the facility scheduled to become operational in the second half of 2027. ICN11 is intended to address growing demand for data center capacity in South Korea, driven by increased adoption of cloud services, connectivity and artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Once operational, the facility will expand Digital Realty’s infrastructure capacity in the country and support customers’ computing and connectivity requirements. The project is being developed with construction partners DPR Construction, DL E&C, Turner & Townsend, and Heerim Architects & Planners.

In a LinkedIn post, Digital Realty described the occasion as “The topping out isn’t just a construction milestone; it’s a powerful symbol of what happens when incredible teams come together to build something bigger than any one of us could achieve alone.”

Readers will recall that during Q2 2021, Digital Realty acquired a five-acre land parcel in Seoul, South Korea for US$ 66 million.

The parcel is located at Gurae-dong, Gimpo City in northwest Seoul, 14 miles from Digital Seoul 1 (ICN10), which was Digital Realty’s first facility in South Korea. Digital Realty’s new land parcel supported the development of the ICN11 facility which has 64 MW of critical IT capacity across 970k sq ft.

According to a Mordor Intelligence report, the South Korea data center market is projected to grow from US$ 1.96 billion in 2025, and US$ 1.99 billion in 2026, to US$ 5.02 billion by 2031, representing a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 20.38 percent between 2026 and 2031. The market is expected to expand from 3.25 thousand MW in 2025 and 3.51 thousand MW in 2026 to 15.88 thousand MW by 2031, registering a CAGR of 35.21 percent over the forecast period.

stories.summary_zh: Digital Realty宣布其在韩国最新的数据中心开发项目ICN11封顶，该设施计划于2027年下半年投入运营。ICN11旨在满足韩国日益增长的数据中心容量需求，这一需求由云服务、网络连接和AI基础设施的日益普及所驱动。[…]
stories.why_zh: 在首尔锁定2027年供应之所以重要，是因为土地和电力限制令都会区新增容量稀缺，而预租通常在交付前很久就已启动。这一里程碑表明，即便竞争者蜂拥进入东京、大阪和柔佛，Digital Realty仍将韩国视为亚太核心增长市场。

stories.title: PLDT defers Vitro REIT IPO to 2027 amid market volatility
stories.summary: Philippines telco PLDT Inc. has postponed the public listing of its data center unit Vitro REIT Inc. to 2027. The deferral is due to unfavorable market conditions and rising interest rates, the firm said in an exchange filing. This would have been the country's first digital infrastructure real estate investment trust listing.
stories.content:
Philippines telco PLDT Inc. has deferred the public listing of its data center unit Vitro REIT Inc. to 2027. The company cited unfavorable market conditions and rising interest rates for the postponement, according to an exchange filing.The initial public offering (IPO) was originally targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. It would have marked the Philippines' first digital infrastructure real estate investment trust (REIT) listing.PLDT stated its continued commitment to the proposed Vitro REIT IPO. The company views it as a key part of its asset monetization and deleveraging plans. The IPO is also intended to support the expansion of the REIT portfolio and the growth of PLDT's data center business.The proposed listing was expected to raise up to US$400 million. It would include Vitro REIT's portfolio of eight Tier 2 and Tier 3 data center assets, totaling 24MW of capacity. The Philippines central bank has raised interest rates three times this year, and headline inflation reached 7.2 per cent in September.

- Investments & Deals

# PLDT defers Vitro REIT IPO to 2027 amid market volatility

Philippines telco PLDT Inc. has postponed the public listing of its data center unit Vitro REIT Inc. to 2027. The deferral is due to unfavorable market conditions and rising interest rates, the firm said in an exchange filing. This would have been the country's first digital infrastructure real estate investment trust listing.

- Published On Oct 16, 2026 at 01:50 PM IST

## Highlights

- PLDT Inc. postponed its Vitro REIT data center IPO until 2027.
- The deferral is due to current market conditions and rising interest rates.
- The IPO would have been the Philippines' first digital infrastructure REIT.
- Vitro REIT's portfolio includes eight data centers with 24MW capacity.

stories.title: AirTrunk nears deal to sell its Johor data centers for US$1 billion: Report
stories.summary: Blackstone-backed hyperscale data center operator AirTrunk is about to seal a deal to sell its Johor data centers to a group of investors including Malaysian pension fund KWAP at a valuation of about US$ 1 billion, according to Reuters yesterday citing people familiar with the matter. AirTrunk has recently postponed its planned Singapore REIT listing to possibly […]
stories.why_it_matters: A US$1 billion exit in Johor would set a pricing benchmark for Malaysian hyperscale assets and signal that institutional capital such as pension funds is moving from passive exposure to direct ownership. It also reshapes AirTrunk's portfolio strategy at a moment when its postponed REIT listing leaves questions about how it will fund its regional pipeline.
stories.content:
Blackstone-backed hyperscale data center operator AirTrunk is about to seal a deal to sell its Johor data centers to a group of investors including Malaysian pension fund KWAP at a valuation of about US$ 1 billion, according to Reuters yesterday citing people familiar with the matter.

<u>AirTrunk</u> has recently postponed its planned Singapore REIT listing to possibly early next year citing market volatility and uncertainty over US interest rates. The IPO which could raise US$1.5 billion, was originally planned for launch in September or October.

Blackstone and KWAP declined to comment, as per Reuters.

Blackstone is a US alternative asset manager which owns QTS, a US data center operator, and has investments in Digital Realty and CoreWeave. It manages US$ 1.3 trillion as of June 2026 making it the largest alternative asset manager in the world.

stories.title: Q&A | APAC’s mature hubs are reinventing themselves around AI-ready, high-density capacity: Mikhail Jaura, JLL

stories.content:
APAC’s data center landscape is diverse, with each economy showcasing unique opportunities and strengths. To better understand what lies ahead for the region’s digital infrastructure industry, we caught up with Mikhail Jaura, JLL’s newly appointed Head of Data Center Research for Asia Pacific.

##### Q-1) In your opinion, what is the single most exciting aspect of APAC’s cloud and data center market?

Mikhail Jaura: What excites me most is that APAC is no longer one story. Five years ago the regional narrative was essentially Singapore, Tokyo and Hong Kong. Today we have a genuinely multi-speed region. Mature hubs are reinventing themselves around AI-ready, high-density capacity. Markets like Johor, Batam, Mumbai, Chennai and Seoul’s periphery are being built at hyperscale. A further tier of countries is putting in its first serious cloud infrastructure. Each market has a different mix of power, land, policy and demand. For investors and occupiers, that diversity is both an opportunity and a challenge.

##### Q-2) Despite exorbitant costs, Japan and Hong Kong remain strong digital infrastructure markets. But do you foresee a slowdown or a correction in the next few years due to other factors like labour shortages, difficulty in acquiring powered land, sustainability concerns etc.?

Mikhail Jaura: Demand fundamentals in both markets remain resilient. In Japan, demand is strong, driven by cloud and AI adoption across a large domestic enterprise base, and supply is not keeping pace. In Hong Kong, sentiment has improved this year on the back of demand from Mainland Chinese hyperscalers, as the market positions itself, through the Northern Metropolis, as the connectivity gateway to the Greater Bay Area.

The constraints are real, though. In Japan, grid connection timelines reaching ten years in Greater Tokyo and Osaka, construction cost inflation, and a construction labour market squeezed by overtime caps since 2024 and a shrinking workforce are lengthening delivery schedules. That is pushing development toward secondary regions such as Hokkaido and Kyushu, supported by government efforts to co-locate power and digital infrastructure.

In Hong Kong, powered land is the binding constraint, which makes government land allocation in the Northern Metropolis important. Absorption slowed in 2025 but has since rebounded, driven by AI demand from Mainland Chinese technology firms. Little new supply arrives before Sandy Ridge, which is over 200 MW, and targeting phased operations from mid-2027, and Goodman’s HKG10 in early 2028. The bigger risks are execution and concentration: projects slipping on power, demand sitting with a few large tenants, and exposure to changes in chip trade rules.

##### Q-3) China has always marched to the beat of its own drum. How do you see the AI story unfolding in China, and how will it impact the wider Asian data center landscape?

Mikhail Jaura: China is building a largely self-contained AI stack. That stack spans domestic accelerators, its own models, and national compute programmes such as “East Data, West Computing”. Launched in 2022, that programme designates eight national computing hubs and ten data center clusters, moving new capacity toward western provinces where land, renewable power and cooling are cheaper.

Chinese labs now produce many of the most widely used open-weight models. Alibaba’s Qwen family recorded more than three billion downloads on Hugging Face, and many large Chinese releases carry permissive licences that allow commercial use.

Further afield, Chinese cloud and internet platforms are among the groups expanding in Southeast Asia, alongside US and regional operators, particularly in Malaysia and Thailand. Chinese cloud providers are also building out regional capacity. For host markets, this investment sits alongside large commitments from US hyperscalers. Governments are welcoming both while working within global trade rules; last year, for example, Malaysia introduced permits for the export and transshipment of US-made AI chips.

##### Q-4) How do you see the hyperscale ecosystem evolving over the next few years in different APAC markets, especially South Korea, Malaysia, and Indonesia?

Mikhail Jaura: South Korea is moving from a Seoul-centric market to national AI infrastructure. Grid capacity in the capital region is increasingly constrained, and new transmission lines and local approvals are taking longer to secure. Policy is pushing new capacity south. The AIDC Special Act, passed in May 2026 and scheduled to take effect in Q1 2027, will fast-track permitting outside Seoul, and regional electricity pricing proposed in August 2026 would offer discounts of up to about 10% in the south.

Malaysia’s Johor capacity has grown more than 50-fold since 2020, with a further 1,800 MW under construction. The next phase is about quality and location. Greater Kuala Lumpur is becoming a cloud market in its own right: Microsoft’s Malaysia West region went live there in 2025, AWS operates a region, and Google is building its first Malaysian data center at Elmina. Malaysia approved over RM 30 billion of data center and cloud investment across dozens of projects in Q1 2026 alone. Power is the gating factor.

Indonesia has a large digital economy, data localisation rules and hyperscaler cloud regions in Greater Jakarta, and Batam offers a cross-border option alongside Johor for demand spilling over from Singapore. Grid reliability, renewable availability and regulatory clarity will decide how fast it scales. Earlier this year, CoreWeave entered the APAC market by announcing three new data center facilities in Indonesia, delivering 360 megawatts of contracted IT power.

##### Q-5) What exciting development trends have you observed regarding enterprise demand in APAC? What are some secondary and emerging markets you are watching keenly?

Mikhail Jaura: Enterprise demand is maturing toward hybrid and multi-cloud architectures. Regulated, latency-sensitive and AI inference workloads are staying in colocation near cloud on-ramps. Data residency is a major driver.

In India, vacancy fell to a record 2.8% in H1 2026, with Mumbai’s growth driven mainly by domestic demand, as residency rules bring workloads onshore. In Australia, sovereign hosting requirements keep government and regulated workloads in the country.

The markets I’m watching most closely include Mumbai, which is expected to take 35 percent of India’s 4.4 GW pipeline by 2029. Also, Chennai where colocation power costs are around 8.4 US cents per kWh, against 18.1 cents in Singapore. In Australia, I’m watching Western Sydney, Melbourne and Australia’s regional markets keenly. Brisbane, Perth, South Australia and Tasmania are attracting AI campuses where power is easier to secure.

I also have my eye on Greater Kuala Lumpur which is maturing into a cloud region as Johor takes the large-scale AI build. Then there are Japan’s GX regions: Hokkaido, Kyushu and Toyama. And let’s not forget Hong Kong, which is an established market that appears on the cusp of a rebound, as it repositions as the connectivity gateway to the Greater Bay Area, whilst still holding a strategic position by servicing enterprise demand from multinational corporations.

##### Q-6) While operators are focusing on acquiring AI chips, do you think they are also planning for their entire lifecycle? What happens after their accounting life ends?

Refresh cycles have compressed sharply. AI accelerators that used to be refreshed roughly every seven years are now refreshed in as little as 13 months. That doesn’t mean older chips are stranded. The newest chips go to frontier model training, and older generations shift to inference and fine-tuning, where cost per token matters more than peak speed.

Inference demand is growing fast enough to keep them booked. Earlier-generation accelerators are still in active service years after launch, which suggests their useful life can run longer than headline refresh cycles imply. For real estate, the pressure point is the building. A facility typically has 18 to 36 months before it needs a major power or cooling upgrade to host the next generation, so the priority is designing facilities flexible enough to support several chip generations over their lifetime.

##### Q-7) The “power struggle” is real! In your opinion, are captive power generation units going to become more common? If so, will we see more on-site generation and dedicated direct supply from such units, or will grid offsets become more popular?

Mikhail Jaura: I think captive and dedicated power will become more common, but policy is already setting the model market by market. For example, in Australia, new national and state frameworks may require hyperscale and AI operators to underwrite new renewable generation and storage at least equal to their added load, and to pay for the associated network upgrades. Meanwhile, in Japan, GX subsidies covering up to 50 percent of capex are available only to projects running entirely on decarbonised local power, effectively tying data centers to nearby generation.

In South Korea, regional tariffs and grid-impact assessments are steering large loads to where generation already sits. While in Singapore, the 700 MW low-carbon data center park on Jurong Island links new capacity allocations to low-carbon energy pathways. Then there’s India, where group captive and open-access renewable models are already well established.

The dominant model will be hybrid. The grid stays the backbone, supplemented by dedicated renewables, on-site generation for speed, and storage. Grid offsets still matter for ESG reporting, but they don’t solve physical power availability, and speed-to-power is now the deciding site selection factor.

##### Q-8) How is water access impacting leasing choices, given protests over data center water consumption in water-stressed markets?

Mikhail Jaura: Water has moved from an ESG footnote to a permitting criterion. For example, Johor has enforced tighter controls that restrict development of Tier 1 and Tier 2 facilities. In Australia, new frameworks restrict the use of potable water for cooling and require recycled or alternative sources. Developers are expected to fund the dedicated water infrastructure their projects need. Meanwhile in Thailand, water is one of the areas being reviewed by the subcommittees drafting national standards during the nation’s temporary pause on data center projects.

For leasing, hyperscale occupiers now ask detailed questions about cooling design, water usage effectiveness (WUE) and water sourcing at the RFP stage. There is a trade-off: moving away from evaporative cooling saves water but can increase power use. The shift to direct-to-chip liquid cooling for AI generally helps on both counts, particularly in closed-loop systems that recirculate the same coolant and need little or no make-up water. That is still not widely understood outside the industry. Sites that depend on contested municipal water will face longer approvals, while those with access to recycled or industrial water are better placed.

Water is also part of a wider question of social licence. Community pushback on data centers has become a contentious issue in the US, and that scrutiny is now reaching APAC.

stories.title: Malaysia's data centre market projected to grow 33% CAGR from 2025-2030 — S&P Global Ratings
stories.summary: Malaysia’s data centre market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 33%t from 2025 to 2030, according to S&P Global Ratings.
stories.why_it_matters: A growth projection of this scale from a ratings agency gives lenders and institutional investors cover to underwrite Malaysian projects, further accelerating capital inflows. It also sharpens the stakes on execution: power supply, water access, and grid upgrades must keep pace, or the pipeline of announced capacity will stall before delivery.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 16): Malaysia’s data centre market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 33%t from 2025 to 2030, according to S&P Global Ratings.

S&P Global Ratings director of corporate ratings Ng Yi Jing said Malaysia has been a fast-growing data centre market in the region, benefiting from both strong underlying demand and spillover demand from Singapore, which has limited land and utilities.

“Now, after several years of strong growth, Malaysia's data centre growth has hit a reset mode because of tighter regulations,” Ng said in a webinar “Digital Infrastructure: Global Financing Trends and the Asia-Pacific Outlook” on Friday.

She said several years of rapid data centre growth also strained Malaysia’s power and water sectors.

“Indonesia and Thailand will benefit from this spillover demand from Singapore, and increasingly Malaysia,” Ng said.

Meanwhile, S&P Global Ratings managing director and head of global infrastructure and project finance Pablo Lutereau said global artificial intelligence (AI) capital expenditure spending will exceed US$1.3 trillion in 2027 versus US$870 billion in 2026 and US$470 billion in 2025.

He said companies’ internal workloads, including Microsoft CoPilot, and multiyear contracts with AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, AI-native companies and enterprises, have supported AI demand.

Lutereau said global data centre demand is expected to grow significantly through 2030, with AI inference projected to record the fastest growth at a 35% CAGR from 2025 to 2030, followed by AI training at 22% and non-AI workloads at 11%.

He said hyperscalers’ off-balance-sheet debt is rising as major technology companies expand their data centre and AI infrastructure investments.

According to S&P Global Ratings, Microsoft recorded the highest future lease obligations at US$329.1 billion (RM1.34 trillion) as of June 30, 2026, followed by Meta at US$279 billion, Oracle at US$260 billion and Amazon at US$137.2 billion.

As of June 30, 2026, Microsoft recorded the highest debt capacity at US$161.5 billion, followed by Alphabet at US$200.6 billion, Meta at US$109.2 billion, Amazon at US$80.7 billion, SpaceX at US$78.5 billion and Oracle at US$32.4 billion.

stories.title_zh: S&P Global Ratings：预计2025-2030年马来西亚数据中心市场复合年增长率达33%
stories.summary_zh: 根据S&P Global Ratings的数据，马来西亚数据中心市场预计在2025年至2030年间以33%的复合年增长率（CAGR）增长。
stories.why_zh: 评级机构给出如此规模的增长预测，为贷款方和机构投资者承销马来西亚项目提供了依据，将进一步加速资本流入。这也提高了执行层面的风险敞口：电力供应、水资源和电网升级必须跟上步伐，否则已公布的容量管线将在交付前陷入停滞。
